status.note: Held by Iraqi forces from May 1948 (the Iraqi front in the northern West Bank).

Under Article VI of the Israel-Jordan armistice signed at Rhodes on 3 April 1949, Jordan's forces replaced the Iraqi forces in this sector in spring 1949; Jordan annexed the West Bank in April 1950, an annexation recognised by few states.

Captured by Israel in the Six-Day War (June 1967) and placed under Israeli military administration. Much of the town was demolished and its residents were temporarily displaced: according to the UN Secretary-General's Special Representative (report A/6797, Sept. 1967), Qalqilya was a town of some 13,000 to 14,000 inhabitants; Jordanian complaints to the Security Council claimed that 12,000 people from Qalqilya were living in the open around 22 June. The Arab mayor told the Special Representative's assistant that most residents had left before and during the fighting and about one quarter remained; the remaining population was advised by the Israeli military commander to leave, was taken to Azun and then Nablus, and was allowed back after three weeks, finding about 850 of some 2,000 dwellings demolished. The Israeli military governor said the destruction was caused partly by tanks and partly by dynamite (houses used for sniping, and others for safety or sanitary reasons); Israel's letter to the Security Council (S/8013) said Qalqilya was a concentration point of the Jordanian attack, that the inhabitants left before Israeli troops arrived, and that only houses where Jordanian troops were found were damaged. Affected populations: the Palestinian (Jordanian-administered West Bank) residents of Qalqilya, plus residents of nearby villages such as Beit Awa and Beit Mersim, which the same report records as demolished; the Israeli and Jordanian sources differ on the cause and extent of the destruction.
Transferred to Palestinian Authority civil and security control (Area A) under the Oslo II Interim Agreement. Israeli troops withdrew on 16 December 1995.
